meaning: Used to express that an action is straightforward and the desired result will be achieved quickly.
examples: Just plug the lead in, hit the power button, and Bob's your uncle.
Add two spoons of sugar, stir well, and Bob's your uncle.
Enter your registration number, tap submit, and Bob's your uncle.
Follow this road to the roundabout, take the first exit, and Bob's your uncle.
Download the installer, click run, and Bob's your uncle.
Put the dough in the oven for twenty minutes, and Bob's your uncle.
Restart your phone after updating, and Bob's your uncle.
Sign the contract at the bottom, and Bob's your uncle, it's official.
Clip the buckle into place, and Bob's your uncle, you're secure.

idiom: Throw a spanner in the works
meaning: To disrupt, prevent, or complicate a plan or process unexpectedly.
examples: The rail strike threw a spanner in the works for our London visit.
Losing my notes right before the tutorial threw a spanner in the works.
A sudden power cut threw a spanner in the works while compiling.
Rain on sports day always throws a spanner in the works.
His unexpected resignation threw a spanner in the works of the team.
The cancelled flight threw a spanner in the works of our holiday.
A software glitch threw a spanner in the works during testing.
Budget cuts threw a major spanner in the works for the laboratory.
Her sudden illness threw a spanner in the works for the theatre production.

meaning: Extremely pleased, proud, and thoroughly delighted.
examples: He received his exam results and was absolutely chuffed to bits.
I was chuffed to bits when our application was accepted.
The cricket team was chuffed to bits after winning the trophy.
She was chuffed to bits with the present her brother picked out.
The tutor praised his historical essay, leaving him chuffed to bits.
We were chuffed to bits with how the new house turned out.
He was chuffed to bits to find an authentic first edition book.
The coach was chuffed to bits with the squad's performance.
My father was chuffed to bits to receive his long-service badge.

meaning: Not aligned with one's personal tastes, interests, or preferences.
examples: Historical fiction is fine, but it is not really my cup of tea.
I accompanied him to the match, but golf is not my cup of tea.
Heavy metal music has never been my cup of tea.
Waking up at dawn for morning runs is not my cup of tea.
Spicy meals are great, but sweet desserts are not my cup of tea.
Working an office desk job is simply not his cup of tea.
Going to noisy crowded clubs is not her cup of tea.
Documentaries about finance are definitely not my cup of tea.
Social media debates are not my cup of tea.

idiom: Cost an arm and a leg
meaning: Extremely expensive; demanding an exorbitant amount of money.
examples: Flagship smartphones cost an absolute arm and a leg nowadays.
Renting a flat in central London will cost an arm and a leg.
Getting high-speed broadband to remote cabins costs an arm and a leg.
Flight tickets during holiday periods cost an arm and a leg.
Repairing the engine on an imported car costs an arm and a leg.
Eating out at five-star restaurants costs an arm and a leg.
Tailor-made wool suits often cost an arm and a leg.
Private hospital treatment without insurance costs an arm and a leg.
Replacing a cracked laptop screen can cost an arm and a leg.

meaning: Making a false assumption, following a mistaken line of thought, or accusing the wrong person.
examples: If you think I broke the window, you are barking up the wrong tree.
The investigators were barking up the wrong tree until fresh clues emerged.
He blamed the hardware, but he was barking up the wrong tree—it was software.
Asking a history major for advanced calculus help is barking up the wrong tree.
You are barking up the wrong tree if you expect him to lend you his car.
The police quickly realized they had been barking up the wrong tree.
Blaming the goalkeeper for that goal is barking up the wrong tree.
She was barking up the wrong tree when assuming he was upset with her.
He searched the styling rules, barking up the wrong tree entirely.

meaning: Feeling slightly ill, fatigued, or low in physical energy.
examples: I cannot attend the tutorial today as I am feeling under the weather.
He looked pale and admitted he had been under the weather all morning.
A warm cup of herbal tea helps whenever you are under the weather.
She stayed home with a hot water bottle because she felt under the weather.
The tutor noticed several students were under the weather after the storm.
I was feeling under the weather, so I skipped cricket practice.
Travelling twelve hours on the coach left him feeling under the weather.
Rest well and stay hydrated while you are under the weather.
He sounded a bit under the weather when we spoke on the phone.

meaning: Bursting with lively energy, enthusiasm, and high spirits.
examples: Despite sleeping only five hours, he arrived at college full of beans.
The schoolchildren were full of beans even after the long walk.
Our dog is always full of beans when let out into the garden.
The young bowler was full of beans during his opening overs.
A cup of strong black tea left him full of beans.
She sounded full of beans after receiving her promotion news.
The squad looked full of beans ahead of the tournament opener.
You look full of beans today; what cheerful news did you get?
Grandfather walked three miles and remained completely full of beans.
